title: Monopoly Round-Up: Goodbye AI Bubble, Hello Real Economy
author: Lee Hepner
content:
As usual, there was a lot of corporate power-related news last week. Hollywood
super-agents launched a campaign to break up the streamers, Dems are musing on
doing corporate oversight after the midterms, and the Trump DOJ wants to
settle the Apple antitrust case.

But before getting to the full round-up, I want to discuss the deflating AI
bubble. There were three important and related pieces of news this week on
that phenomenon, two you may have noticed, and one you probably didn't. The
first is the slide in AI stocks, which we sort of
[predicted](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/monopoly-round-up-the-
cockroaches) last week. That fall was led by the "neoclouds," which are
essentially off-balance sheet entities for big tech firms run by scammers.
That suggests the AI bubble is popping, or is at least in its latter stages.

The second is the government released data showing wholesale prices went up by
a red hot 6.3% last month. And the third is that China put in [new
rules](https://www.geopolitechs.org/p/china-imposes-temporary-export-
registration) to limit exports on key technologies and machines in everything
from solar panels to biotech to chips and AI. Few noticed that, even though it
will likely lead to the de-industrialization of key parts in the U.S.
manufacturing and pharmaceutical base.

These are linked in an important way. The AI Bubble is leading to higher
prices across the board, as capital and material are sucked into this massive
build-out. Meanwhile, the Chinese decision matters profoundly for our future,
but it went almost completely unnoticed because we are so obsessed with AI and
the financial markets. The biggest cost of the AI Bubble, in other words, is
the political focus of the nation is on the problems that don't matter to
anyone except financiers. And it's why we should pop this damn AI bubble as
soon as we can. The longer it goes on, the longer this ridiculous air of
unreality continues.

And with that, let's get to what happened this week. Last Sunday, we discussed
Wall Street's [revolt](https://mattstoller.substack.com/p/monopoly-round-up-
the-cockroaches) against Nvidia-backed Firmus as an early sign the air is
being let out of the AI bubble. On Wednesday, Wall Street tanked _another_
Nvidia-backed neocloud, CoreWeave, whose shares plummeted 15% in one day.
Remember, a neocloud is not really a business; it's a shell company that runs
servers and leases them. Many started as bitcoin miners, and then pivoted to
the latest fad of AI training or inference. There's no special sauce, it's
just a financing scheme by a leasing company and a chip vendor circulating
money to each other. CoreWeave bought chips from its own investor, Nvidia, and
then raised more money from the public markets at higher valuations, under the
guise there's some sort of magic involved in running servers.

### AI Is a Giant Rug Pull

That scheme began falling apart last week, as CoreWeave ended down 24%, with
its bonds in distressed territories. Other neoclouds collapsed as well, as did
adjacent firms like Oracle. Microsoft
[abandoned](https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/microsoft-pulls-
out-uk-data-center-deal-with-nscale-telegraph-reports-2026-10-18/) another
neocloud we discussed, Nscale, just yesterday. It's all collapsing.

But what's also happening here is a "rug pull," where insiders promise
something to public investors and then dump their shares on the rubes.
CoreWeave's three co-founders, Michael Intrator, Brian Venturo and Brannin
McBee, have [cashed
out](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-15/coreweave-founders-
shield-fortunes-with-3-3-billion-stock-sales) $3.3 billion in stock since
CoreWeave went public last year, including over $2.4 billion this year alone.
It pays well to pump and dump, a lesson that Intrator learned in his crypto-
mining days before starting CoreWeave. We should reckon with what that
telegraphs to hard working Americans who are seeing their wages flatline.

What makes the CoreWeave news systemic is that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang did a
press tour to say he was still optimistic about the company. On Huang's
optimism, shares immediately
[slid](https://www.forbes.com/sites/antoniopequenoiv/2026/10/16/coreweave-
shares-slide-after-jensen-huang-says-he-is-optimistic-about-ai-firm/) an
additional 11%. CoreWeave alone doesn't matter, but the $5 trillion Nvidia
does. If Huang's attempt to promote the stock has failed, [that's a big
deal.](https://x.com/Ross__Hendricks/status/2110867855294042179)

post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faa30ee68-6215-49d0-bcfc-4a8b1ce1d6b1_1367x446.png)

So it's more red flags for one of the scammier corners of the AI industry. On
Wall Street, there are rumors that multiple hedge funds betting on AI stocks
have collapsed, and that this coming week things should calm down. Maybe.
That's often what happens these days. Corporate booster Jim Cramer sure thinks
so:

But CoreWeave's crash is another data point in flailing investor confidence
that the AI buildout will produce returns.

There's another metric that investors look at that signals a broader wave of
anti-AI sentiment. It's called the ex-AI index, or SPXXAI, and measures the
S&P 500 without the AI companies that have driven much of the broader market's
growth in recent years. This week, the ex-AI index outperformed the S&P 500 by
4.8%, officially the largest spread since 2024. So investors are shifting away
from AI and toward the rest of the market, aka the "old economy."

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3sg_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe504b8c6-c73d-404e-8046-1628912dd5e0_925x519.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3sg_!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe504b8c6-c73d-404e-8046-1628912dd5e0_925x519.png)The
week ending 10/16 saw the largest move away from AI investments in nearly
three years.

Of course, it may be more than a "rotation" of investment. Money managers are
[warning](https://www.wsj.com/finance/stocks/us-death-penalty-execution-
rates-41ea3427) that sustained losses in AI stocks would be "really bad for
the economy." That's because for money managers, the stock market _is_ the
economy. And it used to be the economy for most people was better represented
by wages and perceptions of affordability. And that's still mostly true but,
as BIG [noted](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/what-would-it-look-like-if-
the-ai) in June, a bubble bursting will have lots of indirect and direct
impacts on the economy in dangerous ways.

Until recently, pensions were controlled by institutional intermediaries,
which meant employers and pension trustees managed the investment risk while
workers themselves were more insulated. Today, retirement vehicles like
401(k)'s and IRAs rise and fall with the market, leaving retirement plans more
directly exposed. For this reason alone, we're a lot more vulnerable today to
a market crash than we were a few decades ago.

Aside from the pension shift, a record number of Americans are exposed to the
stock market. According to a 2025 Gallup poll, some 62% of Americans reported
owning stock. Another metric is the percent equities alone make up of all
financial assets held by individuals and non-profit institutions (i.e., the
general public, not institutional investors), and in 2026 that percentage is
sitting at an all-time high of 48.2%. In 1945, that exposure was 22.5%. In
1984, it hit an all time low of 10.7%.

This dynamic creates a toxic pressure. Stock markets are a reflection of
corporate profits, and corporate profits are a reflection of steadily
increasing prices. And the current economic moment instructs Americans that if
they want financial security, they need to invest in the stock market, without
making clear that this also requires setting aside frustration over rising
prices. There's a political trap, where high profits require higher prices,
but higher prices cause political anger.

### Early Voting

The upcoming midterm elections will be a referendum on Trump's handling of the
economy, and if every election since 2006 is instructive, Democrats are likely
to retake control of either the House or the Senate or both. And sure enough,
the early voting numbers look bad for the incumbent party. Trump has been
banking on the fact the stock market has been going gangbusters, while the
ongoing morass of the Iran War is maintaining persistent inflation.

The problem for Trump is that a higher stock market isn't making up for
flatlining wages and pocketbooks being squeezed at the checkout counter. The
other political concern is longer term and existential. Let's say the
Democrats retake the House and the Senate this year, and perhaps also the
Presidency in 2028. The AI bubble may be popping just in time for them to
blamed for a flagging market.

That's why some political commentators, including on the center left like
Derek Thompson and Chris Hayes, are expressing that our political leaders
don't actually have control over commerce. A couple of months ago, Thompson
and Hayes got into an irksome
[discourse](https://x.com/chrislhayes/status/2086936252041908548?s=46) that
stuck with me, and it went something like this: People want prices to come
down, but are unwilling to endure the process for prices to actually come
down, because that process would probably look like a recession. Outside of a
recession, the President and Congress don't really have any power to affect
prices otherwise.

It's irksome for a number of reasons. Interest rates move prices up and down,
particularly around things like mortgages, auto loans, farm loans and so
forth, and so the powerlessness frame ignores that important price-setting
power. State utility boards literally have price setting power over electric
and gas and water bills. But the problem is really ideological; Hayes,
Thompson and too many others embrace an idea that market forces are
inevitable, and therefore commerce is somehow outside the reach of politics.
That's an uninspiring frame in the run-up to the midterms, if not a form of
up-front apologia for the anti-governing class of elected officials.

There's of course an alternative, equally convenient for the avoidant
politician, which is to rely on the Fed to bring down inflation. And the other
big news of the week was the release of a report showing that [inflation hit
3.7%](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cwy8lx3pg4k2o) in September 2026, far
above the Fed's 2% target. So what will the Fed do? Well, they may hike
interest rates at their end-of-October meeting, even though mortgage rates are
already at a crippling 7.5%. And that's because the only tool the Fed seems to
have is one that aims to stem inflation by weakening labor markets. Never mind
the same inflation report showed real wage growth declined--_again_ --for the
[sixth straight
month](https://www.banking.senate.gov/newsroom/minority/senator-warren-
statement-on-september-2026-cpi-and-updated-trumpflation-tracker-data) _._

It's not just interest rates and capital spending on AI. A big factor in
persistent inflation is gasoline prices, which were up 9% in September due to
currently losing a war with Iran. But seeing as gasoline isn't an optional
expense for most people who need it, it's actually a poor measure of consumer
purchase power and a better measure of the fact that people are being totally
squeezed.

Meanwhile, one of the durable outcomes of the pandemic is that consumer
spending now [relies](https://www.wsj.com/economy/consumers/us-economy-
strength-rich-spending-2c34a571) more heavily on the rich than ever. The top
10% income earners are keeping consumer spending afloat, while the bottom 80%
of consumers are seeing their purchase power whittled away. I spend a lot of
time explaining to lawmakers how AI-based and other algorithmic pricing tools
are facilitating that harm by making collusion and market segmentation more
efficient--which are things Congress
[can](https://scanlon.house.gov/news/documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=2011)
[also](https://casar.house.gov/media/press-releases/news-congressman-greg-
casar-introduces-new-stop-ai-price-gouging-and-wage)
[address](https://www.gallego.senate.gov/news/press-releases/gallego-
introduces-bill-to-crack-down-on-surveillance-pricing/). Until then, Bloomberg
[confirms](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-15/wealthy-
shoppers-expected-to-fuel-faster-us-holiday-retail-sales) this trend is poised
to continue through the holiday season.

And where are the top 10% of income earners making their money? Well,
disproportionately from a rip-roaring stock market.

### Let Them Eat AI

Coming back to the news about Chinese export controls, let's be clear that the
AI bubble, and the fantastical amounts of money being played with in the
financial markets, are ephemeral. Actual productive capacity, and the ability
to make real things we need like medicine and food and toys and cars and
personal protective equipment, is what matters in the long-run. Right now, we
aren't paying attention to that, at all. Here is a chart that makes the point:

[![Image](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ncG7!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb85b59cf-5c77-4bcc-97b4-5fe0ac69018e_1946x1946.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ncG7!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb85b59cf-5c77-4bcc-97b4-5fe0ac69018e_1946x1946.jpeg)

So again, let the AI bubble pop. Rather than see it as a harbinger of doom,
recognize instead the political opportunity in weening our broader economy
from its record-high dependence on the stock market, and to re-establish the
link between wage growth and economic health. More importantly, recognize the
value of returning some sort of reality to how our political and financial
leaders must see the world.

And now on to the Good and Bad news of the week, including more fallout from
the blocked Kroger-Albertsons merger as the two sue each other over who
screwed up more, plus restaurants fear publicly opposing a the Sysco-
Restaurant Depot merger because a major food distributor can take away their
Michelin star. Oh and the money people in Hollywood _finally_ notice there's a
problem, after the Paramount-Warner merger closes. More below, for paid
subscribers only.
